title: The Ultimate Clyde Dome Valve Maintenance Guide: Maximizing Uptime
summary: Keep your pneumatic conveying system running flawlessly. Follow this comprehensive maintenance guide for Clyde Dome Valves, covering daily inspections, seal care, and long-term preventative maintenance.
content:
Built Tough, But Not Invincible

The Clyde Dome Valve is engineered to survive in the harshest industrial environments on earth. From handling 200°C boiler fly ash to slicing through abrasive quartz sand, it is the undisputed heavyweight champion of pneumatic conveying valves.

However, because they are constantly exposed to extreme abrasion and high pressures, they are not "install and forget" devices. Neglecting basic maintenance will eventually lead to torn seals, jammed domes, and catastrophic powder blowouts. To maximize the lifespan of your valves and prevent unplanned downtime, follow this comprehensive, time-based maintenance guide.

1. Daily / Weekly Checks: The Quick Sweep

These checks take only a few minutes but are your first line of defense against major failures.

  • Listen for Leaks: While the valve is in the closed and sealed position, listen closely near the top flange. A faint "hissing" sound indicates that either the inflatable seal has a micro-puncture, or the air supply fittings are loose.
  • Check the Air Supply (FRL): Inspect the Filter-Regulator-Lubricator unit on the local pneumatic panel. Ensure the instrument air pressure is stable (typically between 5.5 and 7.0 bar). Most importantly, drain any condensation (water) from the filter bowl. Water in the air lines will chemically degrade EPDM rubber seals and rust internal actuator springs.
  • Verify Limit Switches: Watch the valve actuate during a cycle. Ensure the "Open" and "Closed" limit switches trigger cleanly and their mounting brackets have not vibrated loose.

2. Monthly Inspections: The Deep Look

Once a month, schedule a slightly deeper inspection to verify pneumatic and mechanical health.

  • Actuator Stroke Test: Disconnect the automated PLC signal and manually trigger the solenoid. Watch the pneumatic cylinder or rotary actuator move the dome. The motion should be smooth and powerful. If it shudders, jerks, or stalls, you may have worn actuator seals, a lack of lubrication, or material build-up restricting the dome.
  • Verify Differential Pressure: Check the gauge for the seal inflation circuit. The seal must be inflated to a pressure exactly 0.15 to 0.2 MPa (1.5 to 2.0 bar) higher than the maximum material conveying pressure. If the regulator has drifted, adjust it immediately to prevent the seal from blowing out (over-pressure) or suffering abrasive wear (under-pressure).

3. The 6-Month / Annual Overhaul

During a planned plant outage, you must physically open and inspect the internal wear components.

  • Clean the Cavity: Open the inspection hatch or remove the valve from the line. Thoroughly clean out any hardened material build-up from the bottom of the valve housing and around the trunnion bearings.
  • Inspect the Spherical Dome: Shine a bright light on the metal dome. You are looking for deep scratches, gouges, or areas where the protective coating (like Tungsten Carbide) has worn away. A scratched dome will instantly slice a new rubber seal. If the dome is deeply scored, it must be refurbished or replaced.
  • Bearing Purge & Lubrication: Check the shaft trunnion bearings. Ensure the continuous "purge air" lines are unblocked and actively keeping dust out of the bearings. Repack the bearings with high-temperature grease if required by your specific model.

4. Inflatable Seal Replacement Strategy

The inflatable seal is the primary consumable of the dome valve. Do not wait for it to burst before replacing it.

Track how many cycles or months it typically takes for a seal to fail in your specific application. Implement a preventative replacement schedule before that failure point. When replacing the seal, never install new rubber against a dirty or scratched dome, and always recalibrate the gap using feeler gauges to ensure zero friction during rotation.

Conclusion

A proactive maintenance strategy transforms the Clyde Dome Valve from a reactive repair headache into a highly reliable, long-lasting asset. Keep the air dry, keep the dome smooth, and strictly control the inflation pressure.
